source: Holton, Mackridge & Philippaki-Warburton, Greek: An Essential Grammar, 2nd ed. (Routledge, 2016), upload a92060f7 (PDF pp. 2-11, Glossary of grammatical terms). Copyrighted, no open license: definitions restated in our own words; the book's own short Greek examples kept.
note: The brief did not list a glossary, but it follows the abbreviations in part 3; extracted as an extra file.

terms.definition: See case.
A verb is active when its subject is the one performing the action (contrast passive).
A word giving a property of a noun.
A word of manner, time, place or quantity.
An adverb, or any phrase or clause serving as one.
An adverb alone or modified by another adverb.
The doer of the action of a verb; usually the noun phrase after από with a passive verb.
A consonant made with the blade of the tongue at the ridge behind the upper teeth, such as [n].
The main clause of a conditional sentence, giving what happens if the protasis condition is met.

example.el: Αν έρθεις στο πάρτι, θα δεις τον Γιάννη
example.en: If you come to the party, you'll see John

terms.definition: A word before a noun making it definite (ο, η, το) or indefinite (ένας, μια, ένα).
Whether a verb presents the action as complete (perfective), ongoing or habitual (imperfective), or as past in relation to another time (perfect).
A prefix added to some verb stems in certain past-tense forms.
A noun form made with a suffix, expressing large size or admiration (compare diminutive).
A consonant made with both lips, such as [p] and [m].

The form of a noun, adjective, pronoun, numeral or article showing its syntactic role: nominative for the subject, accusative for the direct object, genitive for the indirect object or possessor, vocative for addressing.
A syntactic unit with at least one finite verb; main clauses can stand alone as sentences, subordinate clauses depend on another clause.
See degree.
A clause completing the meaning of a verb, noun or adjective (see 10.3).
A word introducing a complement clause: ότι, πως, που.
A word made of two words or stems.
A verb form made with θα + imperfect or pluperfect, for actions that would happen under certain conditions; also a sentence expressing a condition.

example.en: I would lose / I would have lost

terms.definition: A word linking phrases or clauses.
The pattern of endings marking number, gender and case.
A verb with only the imperfective aspect.
Greek has four degrees: positive, comparative, relative superlative and absolute superlative.

example.el: ωραίος / ωραιότερος ή πιο ωραίος / ο ωραιότερος ή ο πιο ωραίος / ωραιότατος
example.en: lovely / lovelier / the loveliest / very lovely

terms.definition: A consonant made with the tongue tip at or near the upper teeth: [s], [t], [l].
The perfective non-past form of a verb.
A verb with no active forms but active meaning.
A word that accompanies a noun but is not an adjective or numeral (κάθε, κάποιος, κανένας); most can also act as pronouns.
A noun form made with a suffix, normally expressing small size or affection.
A weak pronoun or noun phrase in the accusative naming what the verb's action is done to.
The development of a second stress on a word stressed on the third syllable from the end when a weak pronoun follows.
A verb form showing both person and number.
A consonant made by one quick contact between two organs, as Greek [r].
The part of a sentence that carries the main stress and the key emphasis or contrast.
A consonant made by air passing between two organs placed very close, such as [f], [v] (contrast plosive).
See case.
An uninflected non-finite verb form functioning as an adverbial.
A noun with an extra syllable in the plural.
The verb form for positive commands.
The imperfective past form of a verb.

example.en: I was writing, I used to write

terms.definition: The aspect presenting an action as ongoing or habitual.
A verb in the third person singular with no subject.
The mood that typically makes a statement judged true or false; negated with δεν and not used with the particles να and ας.
A weak pronoun or noun phrase naming who or what the action is done to or for.

example.el: Της το έδωσα / το έδωσα στη Μαρία
example.en: I gave it to her / to Mary

terms.definition: A noun, adjective or pronoun that does not change form for number, gender or case.
How a declinable word changes form for number, gender, case, person and tense; also the endings that do this.
A verb that does not normally take an object.
Any bilabial or labiodental consonant.
A consonant made with the lower lip and upper teeth: [f], [v].
A verb connecting the subject with its subject predicate, typically είμαι.
The consonants [l] and [r].
See clause.
Any word, phrase or clause that limits the meaning of a noun, verb, adjective or adverb.
The formal contrast showing how the speaker presents information: as fact (indicative), as wish, hope, plan (subjunctive) or order (imperative).
A consonant produced with air through the nose: [m], [n].
See case.
A verb form showing no person or number, especially the form used with έχω to make the perfect.
A word naming a thing, person, place, process or concept.
A noun, alone or with article, adjective, determiner etc., or a pronoun.
A word expressing number; cardinals give quantity, ordinals give order.
A noun phrase or pronoun naming what the subject acts on (see direct and indirect object).
An adjective or noun phrase that refers to an object.
A consonant made with the tongue at or near the hard palate, such as the first sound of χιόνι.
A noun with the same number of syllables in plural and singular.
A verb form used as an adjective.
One of a set of small words: the subjunctive particles να and ας, the future particle θα, and the negatives δεν and μην.
A verb is passive when its subject is the one acted upon rather than the doer (contrast active).
(i) An aspect made from present or imperfect forms of έχω plus the non-finite, for a past action seen in relation to another time; (ii) a tense made from present forms of έχω plus the non-finite.
The aspect presenting an action as complete (contrast imperfective).
A consonant made by sudden release of a complete closure in the vocal tract: [p], [b], [t].
A tense made from past forms of έχω plus the non-finite, for completion before a specified past time.
A word component added to the front of a stem.
A word before a noun phrase indicating time, place or manner.
A word functioning as a noun phrase: strong or weak personal pronouns, or others such as ποιος, κάποιος, κανένας; most other than personal can also be determiners.
The if-clause of a conditional sentence.
A word expressing quantity.
A pronoun, determiner or adverb introducing questions.

example.el: ποιος, τι, πόσος, πού, πότε, γιατί
example.en: who, what, how much, where, when, why

terms.definition: A prefix on some passive perfect participles, usually a repeated initial consonant plus ε.
Concerning meaning.
A verb with only passive forms in the imperfective aspect and only active forms in the perfective.
A syntactic unit expressing a complete meaning, made of one or more clauses.
The sounds [s] and [z].
The perfective past form of a verb.
The part of an inflected word to which prefixes and suffixes are added.
The noun phrase naming the doer of an active verb or the undergoer of a passive verb.

example.el: Ήρθε η Μαρία / Η Μαρία τραυματίστηκε

terms.definition: An adjective or noun phrase referring to the subject via a linking verb.
The mood presenting the action as wished for, hoped for, expected or planned; marked by να and ας and negated by μην.
See clause.
A word component added to the end of a stem.
See degree.
Concerning how words and phrases are joined into phrases, clauses and sentences.

The grammatical property of a verb referring chiefly to the time of the action; the book distinguishes general categories (past, non-past) from specific forms (present, imperfect, simple past, future, perfect).
The person or thing about which something is said (contrast focus).
A verb that may take an object.
A consonant made with the back of the tongue at the soft palate: [k], [g].
A word denoting an action or state.
See case.
See active and passive.
A consonant produced with vibration of the vocal cords: [d], [m], [v], [z].
A consonant produced without vibration of the vocal cords: [t], [f], [s].
